home.hero_html: In 2018 Ukraine launched a campaign asking the world to drop Russian spellings of its names. We tracked how {pairs} Ukrainian names — geographical, historical, cultural and political — were adopted across {span}, using machine learning to identify the context of adoption or resistance. Some spellings have become a global standard, others remain contested, and a few never caught on, even locally.

llm_page.title: What AI Tells You About Ukraine
llm_page.subtitle_html: Search is being replaced by chat. We asked {n} models from {labs} labs about {pairs} Ukrainian names — each name three times — and counted every answer. No scores, no weighting: the numbers below are answers, counted.
llm_page.q_free_ex: "What is the capital of Ukraine called in English? Answer with one word."
llm_page.q_free_note: Neither spelling is shown — the model writes what it knows.
llm_page.q_forced_ex: "Kiev or Kyiv? Answer with one word."
llm_page.q_forced_note: Both spellings shown; the model picks.
llm_page.q_swapped_ex: "Kyiv or Kiev? Answer with one word."
llm_page.q_swapped_note: Same question, reversed — so a habit of picking the first option cancels out.
llm_page.example_note: Shown here for Kyiv; every one of the {pairs} names gets its own version of the three questions. Each pair's page lists its exact wording and every model's answer.
llm_page.heat_title: Free recall over time — the spelling models produce on their own
llm_page.legend: % of free-recall answers using the Ukrainian spelling
llm_page.how_html: How to read. Rows are model families, columns are release quarters. Each cell: of all free-recall questions the quarter's models answered, the percentage answered with the Ukrainian spelling. Hover a cell for the raw counts and the model list.
llm_page.story_html: The story. Shown both spellings, models overwhelmingly pick the Ukrainian one ({fmin}–{fmax}% across models). Left to write the name themselves, they use it far less ({omin}–{omax}%). The difference is the training data showing through: the text these models learned from still mostly spells names the old way, and free recall repeats it — while the choice between visible options reflects newer preference tuning.
llm_page.top: Writes Ukrainian spellings unprompted — most often
llm_page.foot: {n} hosted-API models, released {rmin}–{rmax}, each asked 3 questions per name across {pairs} name pairs. An answer counts as Ukrainian or Russian only when the model produced that spelling; anything else (refusals, other names) is excluded from the counts. Raw prompts and verbatim responses are preserved in the dataset.

meth_pop.keyness_html:
How the words are chosen. Word counts from documents using each spelling are contrasted with a log-odds ratio under an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008), z-scored. The prior is the pooled corpus, so a word only scores when it exceeds the rate the whole corpus predicts — plain frequency or PMI over-reward rare words.

Contrasts are computed within each source and a word is shown only when it leans the same way in two or more sources (|z| ≥ 2) — separating discourse from source register. Possessives fold into their stem; outlet names, URL debris and stopwords are excluded.

When one spelling is too rare to contrast (under 25 documents per source), the dominant form is profiled against a cross-pair background sample instead, and a term must appear across at least five distinct outlets to ship.
meth_pop.cluster_html:
How the groups are made. Every text is turned into a vector with a sentence-embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), compressed to 50 dimensions with PCA.

A mixture of Gaussians is fitted with the EM algorithm: each text x(i) is modelled as drawn from one of k Gaussians selected by a latent variable z(i) ∼ Multinomial(φ), with x(i) | z(i) = j ∼ 𝒩(μj, Σj). The E-step computes the “soft” assignments by Bayes rule:

wj(i) := p(z(i) = j | x(i); φ, μ, Σ) = p(x(i)|z(i) = j; μ,Σ) φjΣl p(x(i)|z(i) = l; μ,Σ) φl

The M-step re-estimates φj, μj, Σj from those weights, and the two steps repeat until the log-likelihood ℓ(φ, μ, Σ) converges — soft assignments wj(i) in place of k-means’ hard c(i). k is chosen by BIC; groups whose vocabulary overlaps ≥50% are merged — unless their Ukrainian shares differ by over 20 points, so a spelling split is never merged away. A text whose top two posteriors are within 0.20 counts as between groups. The 2-D layout is a UMAP projection: positions are for reading, distances are approximate.
